evidence: ProjectController.create reads input via RequestReader(req.body) with requiredString('name') and optionalString('description'), calls createProject.execute, and responds 201.
UserController.create reads input via RequestReader(req.body).requiredString('name'), calls createUser.execute, and responds 201.
TaskController.create, listByProject and assign all use RequestReader on req.body or req.query, not raw access, and delegate to use cases via TaskUseCases.
TaskController.complete passes req.params.taskId straight to completeTask.execute, with no business logic in the controller.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files are Express HTTP controllers in the infrastructure layer. They have one concern: translate HTTP requests into use-case calls and use-case results into responses. Each one reads input through the shared RequestReader (requiredString/optionalString) and doesn't parse req.body or req.query directly. Each one delegates to application use cases and has no business logic or persistence code. Status codes are used consistently: 201 for creates and 200 for the other actions. TaskController injects a TaskUseCases bundle while the other two inject a single use case. That fits its four use cases and isn't an abstraction bypass. No rule or invariant is duplicated across the files. The repeated `new RequestReader(...)` pattern is just consistent use of the module's abstraction.
